turns.prompt_text: Let's find every single possible way to solve a standard 3 by 3 by 3 Rubik's Cube As well as every heuristic
turns.response_html:
Here's my plan to tackle that topic. Let me know if you need to make changes.

(1) Research and compile all major human-solving methods for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube, ranging from beginner methods like Layer-by-Layer to advanced speedsolving frameworks.
(2) Detail the steps, mechanics, pros, cons, and algorithm counts for advanced speedcubing methods, specifically CFOP, Roux, ZZ, Petrus, and Heise.
(3) Investigate specialized solving methods, including blindfolded techniques (like Old Pochmann, M2, and 3-Style) and Fewest Moves Challenge (FMC) strategies.
(4) Identify computer-based and mathematical solving algorithms, exploring Thistlethwaite's algorithm, Kociemba's Two-Phase algorithm, and Korf's optimal solver, along with the concept of God's Number.
(5) Examine physical and mental heuristics used in speedcubing, such as fingertricks, lookahead, color neutrality, and inspection analysis.
(6) Compare and contrast the human methods based on ease of learning, memorization requirements, execution speed, and mechanical efficiency.
(7) Synthesize the findings into a comprehensive structured overview of Rubik's Cube methodology, categorized by target skill levels and specific solving goals.

I've completed your research. Feel free to ask me follow-up questions or request changes.


Comprehensive Taxonomy of Rubik's Cube Solving Methodologies and Computational Heuristics

The standard $3 \times 3 \times 3$ Rubik's Cube is a highly complex twisty puzzle that can be modeled as a mathematical group $G$ acting on a set of physical components called "cubies" [cite: 1]. Consisting of 8 corner pieces, 12 edge pieces, and 6 fixed center faces, the puzzle generates a state space of approximately $4.3 \times 10^{19}$ unique permutations [cite: 1, 2]:

$$\lvert S \rvert = \frac{8! \cdot 3^7 \cdot 12! \cdot 2^{11}}{2} = 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 \approx 4.3 \times 10^{19}$$

The algebraic structure of the Rubik's Cube group is defined by the generators corresponding to its six faces [cite: 2]. Navigating this state space to find a path from any scrambled configuration to the identity state (the solved puzzle) requires either human-executable heuristics or machine-optimized graph-search algorithms [cite: 2]. This report analyzes the complete landscape of solving systems, human cognitive heuristics, computational reduction models, and machine learning architectures.

Mathematical Foundations and Cayley Graph Metrics

To evaluate the efficiency of any solving system, one must establish the turn metric. The chosen metric alters the path distance (move count) on the Cayley graph of the Rubik's Cube group [cite: 3]. The primary metrics utilized in puzzle theory are detailed below [cite: 3, 4, 5]:

  • Half-Turn Metric (HTM): Any turn of any face by any angle ($90^\circ$ or $180^\circ$) counts as one move [cite: 3, 4]. Slice turns (moving a middle layer) count as two moves [cite: 4, 5].
  • Quarter-Turn Metric (QTM): Only $90^\circ$ face turns count as a single move [cite: 4, 5]. A $180^\circ$ turn counts as two moves [cite: 3, 4, 5].
  • Slice-Turn Metric (STM): Both outer face turns and inner slice turns count as a single move [cite: 4]. This metric is highly favored in methods that rely on middle-layer manipulation, such as the Roux method [cite: 4].
  • Snyder Metric: Any parallel, simultaneous movement of layers on the same axis is counted as a single turn [cite: 4]. This is functionally equivalent to the Axial Turn Metric (ATM), which treats quarter, half, slice, and anti-slice turns along a shared axis as a single movement [cite: 4].

The mathematical proof that God's Number is exactly 20 in HTM and 26 in QTM was established in 2010 and 2014 respectively, through exhaustive computational coset reduction [cite: 3, 6]. The superflip pattern, where all corners are solved and all 12 edges are flipped in place, serves as the classic proof-of-concept for the 20-move upper bound in HTM [cite: 1, 5].

Computational Reductions and Group-Theoretic Solvers

Computational approaches to the Rubik's Cube group bypass the visual heuristics used by humans, relying instead on group theory and graph-search algorithms [cite: 2]. These computer solvers reduce the state space by descending through nested subgroups [cite: 3].

Thistlethwaite's Nested Subgroups

Developed by Morwen Thistlethwaite in 1981, this algorithm is the classic example of nested subgroup descent [cite: 3, 7]. The system maps the group $G_0 = \langle U, D, L, R, F, B \rangle$ to the solved state by transitioning through four nested subgroups [cite: 3, 8]:

  1. Phase 1 ($G_0 \to G_1$): Transition to $G_1 = \langle U, D, L, R, F2, B2 \rangle$ by orienting all 12 edges [cite: 8]. This phase uses coset spaces to reduce the state configurations and requires at most 7 moves [cite: 3].
  2. Phase 2 ($G_1 \to G_2$): Transition to $G_2 = \langle U, D, L2, R2, F2, B2 \rangle$ by orienting all corners and positioning the four E-slice (middle layer) edges within the E-slice [cite: 7, 8]. This requires at most 10 moves [cite: 3].
  3. Phase 3 ($G_2 \to G_3$): Transition to $G_3 = \langle U2, D2, L2, R2, F2, B2 \rangle$ by permuting all corners into their correct orbits and aligning the edges into their respective slices [cite: 8]. This requires at most 13 moves [cite: 3].
  4. Phase 4 ($G_3 \to \text{Identity}$): Permute all remaining elements using only half-turns [cite: 8]. This final phase requires at most 15 moves, yielding a cumulative maximum move count of 45 HTM [cite: 3].

Kociemba's Two-Phase Algorithm

Herbert Kociemba optimized Thistlethwaite's model in 1992 by consolidating the process into two phases [cite: 3, 7]. Instead of navigating through five nested groups, Kociemba's algorithm uses a single intermediate subgroup, $G_1 = \langle U, D, L2, R2, F2, B2 \rangle$, which functions as a $3 \times 3 \times 2$ domino [cite: 7, 9].

During Phase 1, the scrambled cube is solved into the $G_1$ subgroup [cite: 7, 9]. In this state, all corners and edges are oriented, and the four E-slice edges are placed within the middle layer [cite: 9]. This is achieved in at most 12 moves using pruning tables optimized by symmetry reduction [cite: 7]. During Phase 2, the puzzle is solved from the $G_1$ state using only the generators of $G_1$ [cite: 9].

The algorithm uses the Iterative Deepening $A^*$ (IDA*) heuristic search [cite: 9]. Although it does not guarantee an optimal solution on its first pass, it quickly produces suboptimal solutions of 20 moves or fewer [cite: 3, 9]. By continuing the search and systematically lowering the move-count threshold, it eventually converges on an optimal path [cite: 3, 9].

Feather's Algorithm and the 4-List Bidirectional Search

Michael Feather's algorithm reduces the scrambled cube into a 3-color state before performing the final solve [cite: 3, 10]. This 3-color reduction corresponds to a double Domino Reduction on two axes [cite: 3, 7]. The standalone Phase 2 setting with an 8-move limit produces highly optimized Half-Turn Reduction (HTR) solutions [cite: 10].

Alternatively, the 4-List algorithm (Shamir's algorithm) uses a meet-in-the-middle bidirectional search [cite: 3]. It stores all possible permutations up to depth 5 in RAM ($621,649$ states) and generates permutations from both the scrambled and solved states up to depth 10, searching for a matching state at their intersection to find solutions within 20 moves [cite: 3].

Artificial Intelligence and Learned Search Heuristics

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have produced neural network-based solvers that find optimal or near-optimal solutions without human domain knowledge [cite: 2, 11].

Korf's IDA* and Pattern Databases

Richard Korf achieved the first optimal solutions for randomly scrambled cubes in 1997 [cite: 3, 11]. Korf used $A^*$ search with large, precomputed look-up tables called Pattern Databases (PDBs) to serve as admissible heuristics [cite: 2, 12].

PDBs store the exact number of moves required to solve a specific subset of the puzzle, such as the 8 corners, or two separate sets of 6 edges [cite: 3, 11]. Because these databases evaluate subproblems while ignoring other pieces, they never overestimate the actual remaining cost-to-go, ensuring the heuristic remains mathematically admissible ($h(s) \le h^*(s)$) [cite: 12, 13].

DeepCubeA and Autodidactic Iteration

DeepCubeA trains a deep neural network to act as a heuristic function $h(s)$ for the $A^*$ search algorithm [cite: 12, 13]. Because finding optimal paths on a graph with $4.3 \times 10^{19}$ states is computationally difficult, the system uses Autodidactic Iteration (ADI) [cite: 2, 12].

In ADI, the network starts with a solved cube and works backward, creating a training dataset by scrambling the puzzle at increasing depths [cite: 12]. The network learns to predict both the optimal distance to the goal and the next move to take (policy) [cite: 2, 14].

Ensuring Admissibility: Calibrated Deep Heuristics

A primary challenge with deep reinforcement learning solvers is that neural network function approximators often overestimate the remaining cost-to-go, violating the admissibility condition required for $A^*$ search to guarantee an optimal path [cite: 12, 13]. To prevent these overestimations, modern machine learning frameworks implement a three-layered defense to enforce admissibility [cite: 12]:

  1. Contractive Admissible Bellman Operator: Binds target values during bootstrapping to prevent approximation errors from propagating [cite: 12].
  2. Asymmetric Loss Function: Skews training predictions toward underestimation, penalizing overestimations more severely [cite: 12, 13].
  3. Post-Hoc Calibration Offset ($\delta$): Shifts predictions downward by a safety parameter $\delta$ to account for local function approximation noise, ensuring empirical admissibility [cite: 12].

The calibration offset shifts the raw neural network output downward, bounded by a simple, analytically-admissible base heuristic $h_0(s)$ (which is $0.0$ for the Rubik's Cube) [cite: 13]:

$$\hat{h}_{\text{calib}}(s) = \max \left( h_0(s), \hat{h}(s) - \delta \right)$$

This calibration offset allows deep learning solvers to achieve near-perfect path optimality on large state spaces [cite: 14].

Graph Search vs. Beam Search vs. Q* Search

Traditional graph search algorithms like $A^*$ maintain a closed dictionary of visited states and select nodes for expansion from a priority queue [cite: 15]. Beam search reduces memory usage by keeping only a fixed number $B$ of promising nodes at each level, trading mathematical completeness for search speed [cite: 15].

To optimize execution on GPUs, modern systems utilize $Q^*$ Search [cite: 15]. While $A^$ evaluates state nodes, $Q^$ search evaluates the edges of the state graph, mapping a state $s$ and action $a$ to an estimated cost [cite: 15]:

$$q(s, g, a) \approx c(s, a) + h^*(T(s, a), g)$$

By using deep Q-networks (DQNs) to evaluate all possible actions in a single forward pass, $Q^*$ search significantly reduces computational overhead, making it highly effective for solving higher-order puzzles like the $4 \times 4 \times 4$ and $5 \times 5 \times 5$ Rubik's Cubes [cite: 14, 15].

Human Speedsolving Architectures: Layer-by-Layer and Algorithmic Variants

Human-executable methods rely on cognitive heuristics that trade mathematical optimality for pattern recognition and ergonomic execution [cite: 2, 3]. These methods are structured to maximize turns per second (TPS) while minimizing move counts and rotation-induced pauses [cite: 16, 17].

The Layer-by-Layer Method (LBL)

LBL is the foundational beginner's method, proposed in its detailed form by Donald Taylor and David Singmaster in 1978 [cite: 18]. The system completes the cube layer by layer, trading algorithmic efficiency for cognitive simplicity [cite: 18].

  1. The Daisy: A common beginner step where the four white edge pieces are placed around the yellow center face to simplify cross alignment [cite: 18].
  2. Bottom Layer Corners: Solving the white face corners to complete the first layer [cite: 18].
  3. Middle Layer Edges: Inserting the four second-layer edges individually using basic orientation sequences [cite: 18].
  4. 4-Look Last Layer (4LLL): Solving the final layer in four distinct steps: orienting edges, orienting corners, permuting corners, and permuting edges [cite: 18, 19]. This can be expanded into an 8-look method by repeating basic algorithms to minimize the number of patterns a beginner must memorize [cite: 18].

Advanced cubers utilize Keyhole F2L to insert middle-layer edges without solving the first-layer corners first, using the empty corner slots as "keyholes" to reduce the move count [cite: 18].

The CFOP Method (Fridrich Method)

CFOP is the most widely practiced speedsolving system in the world [cite: 16]. It is a highly algorithmic, layer-by-layer system proposed around 1981 by several cubers, including René Schoof, John Conway, David Benson, David Seal, Hans Dockhorn, Kurt Dockhorn, Anneke Treep, and Jessica Fridrich [cite: 16].

  1. Cross: The solver forms a cross on the bottom layer, matching four edge pieces with the bottom center and adjacent side centers [cite: 16, 18]. This is typically solved on the bottom to avoid rotations and improve lookahead [cite: 16].
  2. First Two Layers (F2L): The solver pairs the four remaining first-layer corners with their corresponding second-layer edges, inserting them simultaneously into their slots [cite: 16, 18]. This is done using intuitive blockbuilding or 41 standard algorithmic cases [cite: 16].
  3. Orientation of the Last Layer (OLL): The solver orients all remaining pieces on the top layer in a single step using one of 57 algorithms, ensuring the top face shows a solid color [cite: 16, 19].
  4. Permutation of the Last Layer (PLL): The solver permutes the oriented pieces of the top layer using one of 21 algorithms, completing the solve [cite: 16, 19].

Advanced variations include FreeFOP (building the cross and first two layers dynamically), CFCE (orienting corners and edges simultaneously, then permuting them), and Vandenbergh-Harris (VH) / Zborowski-Bruchem (ZB) [cite: 16].

Corner Permutation and Last Slot (CPLS)

CPLS, proposed by Baian Liu in 2009, is an algorithmic system that solves the last F2L slot (typically Front-Right) while simultaneously permuting the last-layer corners and preserving edge orientation [cite: 20]. This leaves the solver with a highly ergonomic, two-generator last layer that can be solved in a single step using 2GLL (84 algorithms) [cite: 20].

CPLS is divided into two main subsets [cite: 20]:

  • CPLC (Corner Permutation Last Corner): Solves the last F2L corner and permutes the last-layer corners (26 algorithms) [cite: 20].
  • CPLE (Corner Permutation Last Edge): Solves the last F2L edge and permutes the last-layer corners (6 algorithms) [cite: 20].

Human Speedsolving Architectures: Blockbuilding and Columns-First Methods

Rather than solving the puzzle layer by layer, blockbuilding methods build up larger blocks of solved pieces dynamically, offering significantly lower move counts [cite: 21].

The Roux Method

The Roux method is a hybrid of blockbuilding and corners-first techniques, proposed by Gilles Roux in 2003 [cite: 22, 23]. It offers a low average move count of approximately 48 moves in STM [cite: 22].

  1. First Block: The solver builds a $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block on the lower-left side of the cube, typically starting with a $1 \times 2 \times 2$ inner square [cite: 22, 24].
  2. Second Block: The solver builds a second $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block on the lower-right side, opposite the first, without disrupting it [cite: 22]. This leaves the U layer and M slice free to move [cite: 22].
  3. CMLL: The solver simultaneously orients and permutes the four remaining top-layer corners using one of 42 algorithms [cite: 22].
  4. Last Six Edges (LSE): The solver completes the remaining six edges (four in the U layer, two in the D layer) using only U and M moves [cite: 22, 25]. This step is further split into:
    • Step 4a: Orient all six remaining edges (EOLR) [cite: 22].
    • Step 4b: Place the UL and UR edges into their correct positions on the left and right faces [cite: 22].
    • Step 4c: Permute the remaining four middle-slice edges [cite: 22, 26].

Advanced solvers use specialized prediction techniques like Straughan Corner Orientation Prediction (tracking top-face stickers during the final moves of the second block) and DFDB Recognition (tracking the DF/DB and UF/UB stickers during LSE) to eliminate pauses between steps [cite: 22].

The ZZ Method

The ZZ method focuses on edge orientation (EO) at the start of the solve, eliminating the need for cube rotations and allowing the rest of the solve to be performed using only ergonomic L, U, and R moves [cite: 17].

  1. EOLine or EOCross: The solver orients all 12 edges while placing either the DF and DB edges (EOLine) or all four D-layer edges (EOCross) [cite: 17].
  2. ZZ F2L: Because all edges are pre-oriented, the solver can build the left and right $2 \times 3 \times 1$ blocks using only ergonomic $\langle L, U, R \rangle$ turns, avoiding any rotations [cite: 17]. This can be done using intuitive blockbuilding, Openslotting, or LRUL/RLUR algorithms to solve diagonal slots simultaneously [cite: 17].
  3. Last Layer: Pre-oriented edges significantly reduce the last-layer state space, allowing the solver to choose from several advanced systems:
    • ZZ-OP: Solved via standard OCLL and PLL [cite: 17].
    • OCELL + CPLL: Orienting corners and permuting edges in one step, then completing the solve with CPLL (ZZ-$\pi$) [cite: 17].
    • ZZ-a: Uses ZBLL, a massive set of 493 algorithms that solves the entire last layer in a single step, provided all edges are pre-oriented [cite: 17, 27].

The Petrus Method and Petrus-W

The Petrus method, proposed by Lars Petrus in 1981, is an efficient blockbuilding system designed to minimize move counts by orienting edges early in the solve [cite: 21, 28, 29].

  1. 2x2x2 Block: Build a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block in one corner of the cube [cite: 21, 29].
  2. 2x2x3 Block: Expand the $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block into a $2 \times 2 \times 3$ block [cite: 21, 29].
  3. Edge Orientation (EO): Orient all remaining edges, restricting the rest of the F2L solve to only L, U, and R moves [cite: 21, 29].
  4. Finish F2L (L2P): Solve the final two corner-edge pairs while preserving edge orientation [cite: 29].
  5. Last Layer (COLL/EPLL): Solve the remaining layer [cite: 21, 29].

The Petrus-W variant modifies the edge orientation to use ZZ-style EO relative to the U, F, and D layers, allowing the final two pairs (L2P) to be solved without rotations [cite: 29]. Solvers can also use CLP to orient and permute corners while completing the final F2L pair, skipping the COLL step [cite: 29].

The Mehta Method

Proposed by Yash Mehta in 2020, this algorithmic method combines blockbuilding with structured decision paths to optimize TPS [cite: 30].

  1. First Block (FB): The solver builds a $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block on the D layer, placing a $1 \times 1 \times 3$ bar at the DL position [cite: 30].
  2. 3-Quarters Belt (3QB): The solver solves three of the E-slice edges relative to their centers [cite: 30].
  3. Edge Orientation + Last Edge (EOLE): The solver inserts the final E-slice edge while orienting all remaining edges using one of 55 cases [cite: 30].
  4. Path Selection: Based on the resulting state, the solver chooses one of five algorithmic paths to complete the solve:
    • Mehta-6CP: Orient the remaining six corners (6CO, 71 algs) $\to$ Permute the six corners (6CP, 47 algs) $\to$ Permute the last five edges (L5EP, 16 algs) [cite: 30].
    • Mehta-APDR: Orient the remaining six corners (6CO, 71 algs) $\to$ Solve the DR block (APDR, 38 algs) $\to$ PLL (21 algs) [cite: 30].
    • Mehta-CDRLL (Main Path): Solve the D-layer corners (DCAL, 80 algs) $\to$ Orient and permute the U-layer corners while leaving the DR edge unsolved (CDRLL, 42 algs) $\to$ L5EP (16 algs) [cite: 30].
    • Mehta-JTLE: Solve the D-layer corners (DCAL, 80 algs) $\to$ Orient the U-layer corners while inserting the DR edge (JTLE, 34 algs) $\to$ PLL (21 algs) [cite: 30].
    • Mehta-TDR (High-Memory Path): Solve the DR block (TDR, 350 algs) $\to$ ZBLL (493 algs) [cite: 30].

The LSFB Method (Light Slice Fire Blocks)

Proposed by Ryan Kennelly for the 2021 Method Development Competition, LSFB is a beginner-friendly blockbuilding system designed to introduce solvers to edge orientation with a minimal algorithm set [cite: 31].

  1. Left Block: Build a $2 \times 2 \times 1$ block on the left side of the cube, similar to the first block in Roux but leaving the front pair open [cite: 31].
  2. Right Block: Build a matching $2 \times 2 \times 1$ block on the opposite right side [cite: 31].
  3. Corner Orientation: Orient the D-layer corners intuitively, then orient the U-layer corners using the 7 standard OCLL algorithms or Mehta's 6CO set [cite: 31].
  4. FLFR + D Corner: Solve the FL and FR edges alongside a D-layer corner [cite: 31]. This is done by orienting and stacking the FL and FR edges on the B face, bringing the D-layer corner into the U layer, and executing a short sequence (e.g., $F^\ M^2\ F^$) to solve all three pieces simultaneously [cite: 31].
  5. Last Six Edges (LSE): Completed using Roux-style LSE [cite: 31].
  6. Last Five Corners (L5C): Solves the remaining five corners in a single step using 16 algorithms derived from ZZ-CT (TTLL cases) and PLL (CPLL cases) [cite: 31].

Specialized, Hybrid, and Direct Solving Frameworks

Beyond the dominant speedsolving methods, several specialized, hybrid, and direct solving frameworks exist, serving niche roles in speedcubing, Fewest Moves, or blindfolded solving [cite: 28, 32, 33, 34].

The Snyder Method

Invented by Anthony Snyder in 1982, this system solves the puzzle by orienting and permuting pieces simultaneously at each stage to optimize move efficiency [cite: 28].

  1. Blockbuilding Start: Form a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block, $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block, or an Xcross [cite: 28].
  2. F2L-1 State: Solve the rest of the F2L, leaving a single slot open [cite: 28].
  3. Last Slot + 1 LL Edge (LS+1E): Solve and insert the final F2L pair while orienting and placing at least one last-layer edge [cite: 28].
  4. Last Layer Edges + 1 Corner (LLE+1C): Orient and permute all last-layer edges plus one corner, leaving exactly three unsolved corners [cite: 28].
  5. Last Three Corners (L3C): Solve the remaining three corners in a single step using commutators or short direct algorithms (e.g., Niklas, Anti-Niklas) [cite: 28, 35].

The Heise Method

The Heise method is an intuitive, algorithm-free system designed for Fewest Moves solving [cite: 21, 24].

  1. Four Heise Blocks: Build four $1 \times 2 \times 2$ blocks that share a common last-layer color [cite: 21, 24].
  2. F2L-1 and Edge Orientation: Align the blocks into an F2L-1 state while orienting the remaining edges [cite: 24].
  3. Solve Edges + Two Corners: Solve the five remaining edges and two corners simultaneously using only L and U moves, leaving exactly three corners unsolved [cite: 21, 24].
  4. L3C Commutators: Solve the final three corners using intuitive commutators [cite: 21, 24].

Advanced variations include Speed-Heise (Matt DiPalma's 72-algorithm set to systemize Step 3) and FLFL (which simplifies Step 3 by solving the final bottom corner separately, leaving the last four corners to be solved) [cite: 24].

Shadowslice Snow Columns (SSC)

SSC is a move-efficient, columns-first speedsolving method proposed by Joseph Briggs and Julien Adam [cite: 34].

  1. EoEdge: Solve an rotated EOLine, placing the FL and BL edges instead of the DF and DB edges [cite: 34].
  2. Corner and Edge Orientation: Orient all corners and the remaining edges while positioning the FR and BR edges [cite: 34]. This is done using intuitive blockbuilding, with the advanced variation utilizing OL5C to orient the remaining five corners in a single step [cite: 34].
  3. Finish the Cube: Complete the solve using one of several variants:
    • EZD Variant: Separates and permutes the remaining edges using a dedicated algorithm set [cite: 34].
    • Broken Variant: Solves the F2L after Step 2 using highly ergonomic $\langle R2, L2, M2, U, D \rangle$ moves [cite: 34].
    • Permute Last Variant: Separates the edges and applies PLL to both the U and D layers, similar to the Belt method [cite: 34].

CEOR and LEOR

CEOR is a rotationless speedsolving method designed for one-handed solving, functioning as a counterpart to LEOR [cite: 23].

  1. CPFB (Corner Permutation First Block): Solve a $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block on the left side while simultaneously permuting all corners [cite: 23]. This is typically done by solving a $1 \times 1 \times 3$ line at DL, then using only U, u, R, and r moves to solve the FL and BL edges and left center [cite: 23].
  2. EOdM: Orient all remaining edges and solve the DF and DB edges [cite: 23].
  3. RB (Right Block): Solve the right side $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block [cite: 23].
  4. 2GLL: Solve the remaining last layer using only 2GLL (84 algorithms) [cite: 23].

CEOR consolidates several historically independent proposals, including Noah's CP Block 2.0, Yash Mehta's YruRU (which includes dedicated corner permutation recognition), Zbigniew Zborowski's C2GR, and 2GR [cite: 23].

Polaris

Polaris is a speedsolving method proposed by James Straughan in 2010 to resolve the ergonomics issues of traditional Orient First and Belt methods [cite: 36].

  1. EOLine on Left: Solve a rotated EOLine, ensuring all edges are oriented and the FL and BL edges are solved [cite: 36].
  2. D/U Blocks: Solve an oriented $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block on the D layer and an oriented $1 \times 2 \times 3$ block on the U layer [cite: 36].
  3. Corner Orientation + E-slice: Orient the remaining four corners on the right side while positioning the remaining E-layer edges (41 algorithms) [cite: 36].
  4. Permutation: Permute all remaining pieces, typically using a COLL variant followed by L6EP [cite: 36].

The Belt Method (Equator/Ring)

Proposed by Denton Holder, the Belt method solves the middle E-slice first, dividing the cube into isolated top and bottom layers [cite: 37].

  1. E-slice: Solve the four middle-layer edges and centers intuitively [cite: 37].
  2. Separation: Separate the remaining pieces into their respective layers, placing all U-color pieces on top and D-color pieces on bottom [cite: 37].
  3. Orientation: Orient the U and D layer pieces individually using OLL [cite: 37]. If orientation parity occurs (e.g., a single unoriented edge in the M layer), it is corrected using specialized parity algorithms (e.g., $M'\ U\ M$) [cite: 37].
  4. Permutation: Permute the U and D layers [cite: 37]. Parity issues (occurring 50% of the time) are corrected using the PLL parity sequence ($M2\ U2\ M2$) before completing both layers with PLL [cite: 37].

A notable variant is the KwS method, which refines the belt separation and orientation steps for improved speed [cite: 37].

Blindfolded Solving (3BLD) and Multicycle Commutators

Blindfolded solving uses cycles of pieces to solve the puzzle without looking, mapping the permutation and orientation of pieces using letter schemes [cite: 38, 39].

Classic Pochmann Method

The Classic Pochmann method is a simple 2-cycle system that solves one piece at a time using a dedicated buffer location and a target location [cite: 40, 41].

  • Corners: The buffer is UFL [cite: 40]. The solver identifies the piece in the buffer and applies setup moves to bring its destination slot to URF [cite: 40]. The solver then applies the Y-Permutation algorithm, which swaps the UFL and URF corners while swapping two edges [cite: 39, 40]. Reversing the setup moves completes the cycle [cite: 40].
  • Edges: The buffer is UR or UL. The solver uses setup moves to bring the target edge slot to the UB or UL position and applies the T-Permutation or J-Permutation algorithm to swap the buffer and target pieces [cite: 39, 40].
  • Parity: If the solve contains an odd number of targets, a corner-edge swap occurs [cite: 40]. This is resolved at the end using the Ra-Permutation algorithm [cite: 39].

The M2/R2 Method

Stefan Pochmann developed this faster 2-cycle system to speed up blindfolded solves [cite: 41].

  • M2 Method (Edges): The buffer is DF [cite: 41]. The solver shoots to target edge slots using specific setup moves combined with the $M^2$ slice turn [cite: 41]. For targets located within the M slice (e.g., UB, UF, BD), specialized algorithms are used to prevent orientation errors [cite: 41].
  • R2 Method (Corners): The buffer is UFR, and the target is DBR [cite: 41]. The solver uses conjugates of the $R^2$ turn to solve corners [cite: 41].

Intermediate 3-Cycle Methods (Orozco and Eka)

These systems solve pieces one or two at a time using short, intuitive 3-cycle commutators, serving as a bridge to advanced methods [cite: 42, 43].

  • Orozco Method: Developed by Gabriel Alejandro Orozco Casillas, this system uses a fixed buffer (e.g., UFR for corners, UF for edges) and a helper position (e.g., URB for corners, UR for edges) [cite: 43]. To solve a letter pair $A B$, the solver executes a commutator cycling $\text{Buffer} \to A \to \text{Helper}$, followed by a second commutator cycling $\text{Helper} \to B \to \text{Buffer}$ [cite: 43]. This solves each target individually using short, efficient commutators [cite: 43].
  • Eka Method: Designed for edge solving, Eka uses the UF buffer and UR helper [cite: 42]. The first target is set up to the UR helper, and the solver executes a 3-style commutator ($\text{Buffer} \to \text{Helper} \to \text{Second Target}$) to solve both pieces simultaneously [cite: 42].

3-Style (Beyer-Hardwick / BH Method)

3-Style is the standard method for elite blindfolded solvers [cite: 39, 44]. It uses pre-memorized, move-optimal 3-cycle commutators to solve pairs of pieces simultaneously, matching orientation and permutation in a single step [cite: 39, 45].

The system uses commutators of the form $A B A' B'$ (denoted $[A, B]$), where $A$ is a 3-move insertion and $B$ is a single-move interchange [cite: 45]. The primary commutator types include [cite: 45]:

  • Pure Commutators: 8-move algorithms of the form $[A, B]$, where the insertion and interchange moves align perfectly without setup moves [cite: 45].
  • A9 / Setup Commutators: 9-move algorithms of the form $[S: [A, B]]$, where a setup move $S$ is applied before the commutator and reversed afterward [cite: 45].
  • Cyclic Shifts: Algorithms used when all three target pieces are on the same layer but cannot be solved using standard insertions [cite: 45].
  • Orthogonals and Columns: Specialized commutators used when pieces are in opposite orbits or require half-turns for alignment [cite: 45].

5-Style Method

The 5-Style method is an advanced blindfolded system designed to solve five pieces simultaneously using 5-cycle algorithms [cite: 44]. By solving five pieces in a single step, the method reduces the total move count of a blindfolded solve to approximately 50 to 70 moves [cite: 44].

To make learning the massive algorithm set manageable, the system uses Yo Notation to represent and memorize 3-generator and 4-generator algorithms [cite: 44]. Solvers also use Letter Quads to consolidate their memorization, reducing the cognitive load during the inspection phase [cite: 44].

Summary of Key Technical and Practical Findings

The development of Rubik's Cube solving systems shows a clear convergence between human cognitive heuristics and computer group-theory reductions. Early speedsolving methods, such as Layer-by-Layer, were purely spatial and physical, designed around visual feedback [cite: 18]. As human performance neared physical limits, advanced speedsolving methods like ZZ and Roux shifted toward algebraic models [cite: 17, 22]. By orienting edges early or splitting the cube into independent blocks, these systems restrict the puzzle's degrees of freedom, allowing solvers to work within smaller mathematical subgroups [cite: 9, 17, 22].

This same subgroup reduction is what allowed early computer solvers like Thistlethwaite's and Kociemba's algorithms to navigate the massive state space of the cube [cite: 3, 7]. Today, these worlds meet in the Fewest Moves Challenge, where human solvers use computer-derived Domino Reduction triggers to find near-optimal paths [cite: 7]. At the same time, machine learning architectures are evolving from simple brute-force search into systems that use calibrated neural networks to learn admissible heuristics, bridging the gap between deep learning and rigorous group theory [cite: 12, 14]. These parallel paths show that whether solved by human hands or computer networks, the key to mastering the complexity of the Rubik's Cube lies in reducing it to its underlying algebraic structures.
